```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message=FALSE, warning=FALSE)
```

This is the 3rd version of the (NOR + baseline) ancestry modeling analysis. It is very similar to the [2nd version](https://github.com/tylermccraney/Puyallup-White/blob/main/ancestry-models2.md) except for a single locus *Ots_u07-07.161* that was removed because of null alleles detected in the [2nd version](https://github.com/tylermccraney/Puyallup-White/blob/main/scripts/delta-fst-test2.R) of $\Delta F_{\text{ST}}$ analyses. The ADMIXTURE plots from version 2 and 3 look identical, but the classifications changed by a few counts.  

#### Genetic Management of White River Spring Chinook Salmon

```{r, echo=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)

rdat <- 
  readRDS("../data/rdat.RDS")

rdat <- 
  mutate(rdat, day=yday(date), assignment=factor(assignment, levels=c("Spring", "Unknown", "Fall")))

day_breaks <- 
  tibble(
    day=c(yday("2024-06-01"), yday("2024-06-15"), yday("2024-07-01"), yday("2024-07-15"), yday("2024-08-01"), yday("2024-08-15"), yday("2024-09-01")),
    label=c("Jun-01", "Jun-15", "Jul-01", "Jul-15", "Aug-01", "Aug-15", "Sep-01"))

ggplot(rdat |> filter(!is.na(day)), aes(x=day, fill=assignment)) + 
  geom_bar(width=1) + 
  labs(title="White River NOR Genetic Stock Assignments 2009-2024", x=NULL) + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=day_breaks$day, labels=day_breaks$label) +
  scale_fill_manual(name=NULL, values=hcl.colors(3))
```

Let's break this plot apart by assignment, bin days, and visualize with free y-scale to get sense of patterns.  

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.height=8, fig.width=4}
ggplot(rdat |> filter(!is.na(day)), aes(x=day, fill=assignment)) + 
  geom_histogram(show.legend=FALSE) + 
  labs(title="White River NORs 2009-2024\nGenetic Stock Assignments", x=NULL) + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=day_breaks$day, labels=day_breaks$label) +
  scale_fill_manual(name=NULL, values=hcl.colors(3)) + 
  facet_wrap(vars(assignment), ncol=1, scales="free_y")
```

#### Ancestry Model
ADMIXTURE is a command-line application that estimates individual ancestry proportions from large SNP datasets. It uses the same model as STRUCTURE, but replaces MCMC sampling with ML optimization, so runs finish in just minutes rather than hours.  

Just like STRUCTURE, ADMIXTURE requires you to specify ${K}$ (the assumed number of ancestral populations) in advance, although it uses cross-validation (CV) to help pick the best ${K}$. For each value of ${K} = 1 - ...$, ADMIXTURE first randomly partitions entries of the genotype matrix into 10 folds, hides 10% of the genotype calls in each fold, fits the ancestry and allele-frequency parameters on the remaining 90%, and measures how accurately those parameters predict the masked genotypes. The CV error is then plotted to see the ${K}$ value with the lowest CV error, which should give us the best statistical fit.  

#### White River NORs & White/Puyallup (Green River Origin) Baseline

We convert the genotype matrix into binary PLINK (.bed/.bim/.fam) format, run ADMIXTURE, and then import the .Q files---containing estimated ancestry fractions per individual---into R for plotting and summary.  

```{r, echo=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)

gdatw <- 
  readRDS("../admixture/gdatw2.RDS")

# remove bad SNP
gdatw <- 
  select(gdatw, -ots_u07_07_161_a1, -ots_u07_07_161_a2)

write_delim(
  mutate(gdatw, ID=paste0("i", ID)), 
  col_names=FALSE, 
  file="../admixture/gdatw3.ped", 
  na="0")

data.frame(Chromosome=1, SNP=paste0("rs", 10001:10251), GD=0, POS=seq(1, 251000000, 1000000)) |> 
  write_delim(col_names=FALSE, file="../admixture/gdatw3.map")
```



```{bash, eval=FALSE}
conda activate admixture_Env

cd /Users/tylermccraney/Google\ Drive/My\ Drive/Puyallup-White/admixture

plink --file gdatw3 --make-bed --out gdatw3

for K in 1 2 3 4; do admixture -s $RANDOM --cv=10 gdatw3.bed $K | tee gdatw3_log${K}.out; done

grep -h CV gdatw3_log* > gdatw3_log.txt
```

Now lets look at the results of ADMIXTURE. The R code is hidden in this page but it can be found [here](https://github.com/tylermccraney/Puyallup-White/blob/main/ancestry-models3.Rmd).  

```{r, echo=FALSE}
gdatw_cv <- 
  read_delim("../admixture/gdatw3_log.txt", col_names=FALSE) %>% 
  mutate(K=1:nrow(.)) |> 
  select(K, CV_error=X4)

plot(gdatw_cv); lines(gdatw_cv)

```

We have clear evidence above indicating that ${K} = 2$ should provide the best statistical fit.  However, it is common practice to plot the runner-up ${K}$ as well, in order to see if any grouping patterns are visible but not accounted for by the best ${K}$. Let's do that so we can see if there's any indication of more than 2 ancestral populations.  

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.width=13, fig.height=6}
tbl2 <- read.table("../admixture/gdatw3.2.Q")

tbl3 <- read.table("../admixture/gdatw3.3.Q")

gdatw_pop <- 
  gsub(pattern="River", replacement="R", gdatw$pop) |> 
  gsub(pattern="Creek", replacement="C") |> 
  gsub(pattern="Hatchery", replacement="H") |> 
  gsub(pattern="Chinook_", replacement="") |> 
  gsub(pattern="Buckley_Trap_", replacement="") |> 
  gsub(pattern="at_", replacement="_") |> 
  gsub(pattern="unclipped", replacement="Fall") |>
  gsub(pattern="_PBT", replacement="Fall") |>
  gsub(pattern="WDFW_FH", replacement="Fall") |>
  gsub(pattern="Spring_Fall_06KK", replacement="Spring_06KK_Baseline") |>
  gsub(pattern="R_24ND", replacement="R_Spring_24ND_Baseline") |>
  gsub(pattern="R_25NI", replacement="R_Spring_25NI_Baseline") |>
  gsub(pattern="fall", replacement="Fall") |>
  gsub(pattern="08HZ", replacement="08HZ_Baseline") |>
  gsub(pattern="98HB", replacement="98HB_Baseline") |>
  gsub(pattern="10JX", replacement="10JX_Baseline") |>
  gsub(pattern="12IP", replacement="12IP_Baseline") |>
  gsub(pattern="__", replacement="_") |>
  gsub(pattern="Hupp_Springs_23LQ", replacement="Hupp_S_Spring_23LQ_Baseline") |>
  gsub(pattern="Minter_C_23LR", replacement="Minter_C_Fall_23LR_Baseline")

rownames(tbl2) <- 
  gdatw$ID

rownames(tbl3) <- 
  gdatw$ID

tbl2$pop <- 
  gdatw_pop

tbl3$pop <- 
  gdatw_pop

tbl2 <- 
  bind_rows(tbl2, tibble(V1=rep(NA, 4), V2=rep(NA, 4), pop=rep(NA, 4)))

tbl3 <- 
  bind_rows(tbl3, tibble(V1=rep(NA, 4), V2=rep(NA, 4), V3=rep(NA, 4), pop=rep(NA, 4)))

rownames(tbl2)[1317:1320] <- 
  paste0("spacer", 1:4)

rownames(tbl3)[1317:1320] <- 
  paste0("spacer", 1:4)

tbl2 <- 
  tbl2[rownames(tbl2)[c(1:225, 1317, 226:966, 1318, 967:1002, 1319, 1003:1060, 1320, 1061:1316)], ]

tbl3 <-

# pdf("../admixture/gdatw3_k2_3.pdf", width=13, height=6)
par(mar=c(7, 4, 4, 2) + 0.1, mfrow=c(2, 1))
barplot(t(as.matrix(tbl2[-3])), col=hcl.colors(3)[-2], ylab="Ancestry", border=NA, names.arg=tbl2$pop, las=2, cex.names=0.3, space=0, main=expression(italic(K)==2*`*`), font.main=1)
abline(v=c(226, 968, 1005, 1064), col="white")
mtext(text="Baseline Spring", adj=0.08)
mtext(text="'Spring'")
mtext(text="?", adj=0.73)
mtext(text="'Fall'", adj=0.77)
mtext(text="Baseline Fall", adj=0.90)
barplot(t(as.matrix(tbl3[c(3, 1, 2)])), col=hcl.colors(3), ylab="Ancestry", border=NA, xaxt="n", las=2, cex.names=0.3, space=0, main=expression(italic(K)==3), font.main=1)
abline(v=c(226, 968, 1005, 1064), col="white")
mtext(text="Baseline Spring", adj=0.08)
mtext(text="'Spring'")
mtext(text="?", adj=0.73)
mtext(text="'Fall'", adj=0.77)
mtext(text="Baseline Fall", adj=0.90)
# dev.off()
```

The barplot for ${K} = 2^*$ shows the best statistical fit, and I don't see any patterns in the ${K} = 3$ barplot that would suggest the presence of more than two ancestral populations.   

#### Interpretation of mixed-color barplots

A mixed-color bar plot does not uniquely prove recent hybridization. Since STRUCTURE/ADMIXTURE clustering algorithms reconstruct allele frequencies by minimizing departures from Hardy-Weinberg and linkage equilibrium, several different evolutionary and demographic scenarios can produce the same patterns in bar plots. Here are a few common examples for White R spring NOR and GRO baseline fall samples that could be difficult or impossible to distinguish:  

1. If recent admixture occurred (true hybridization), White R spring and Green River fall were historically isolated, genetically differentiated parental populations that came into secondary contact and interbred. In this case, White R spring and Green River fall parental populations would appear as solid purple and yellow bars, respectively, while the hybrid population appears as a mosaic of those colors proportional to their genetic contribution.  

2. With ghost admixture (an unsampled source population), White R spring hybridizes with an unsampled or extinct "ghost" population other than Green River fall, though the ghost population shares more ancestry with Green River fall (e.g., Puyallup R fall). This forces the hybrid's alleles to be modeled as a mixture of White R spring and Green River fall, creating a false impression of direct hybridization between the two sampled runs.  

3. With a recent population bottleneck, White R spring and Green River fall diverge from a common ancestor without any subsequent gene flow. White R spring then underwent a severe population bottleneck causing its allele frequencies to shift away from the ancestral state, while Green River fall population remains large and retains ancestral allele frequencies. In this scenario, STRUCTURE/ADMIXTURE would assign the bottlenecked White R spring population its own distinct cluster color and model the un-bottlenecked Green River fall population as an "admixed" intermediate between White R spring and Green River fall, even though hybridization did not occur.  


It would be reasonable to assume all three of these scenarios—recent hybridization, ghost admixture, and population bottleneck—have occurred in with respect to White R spring and Green River fall, further complicating the interpretation of results.  

#### Classify fish as 'Spring', 'Fall', or 'Hybrid' based on their proportional ancestry  

In this section I apply a 80% threshold to classify fish as 'Spring', 'Fall', or 'Hybrid' by their proportional ancestry. Then I compare the classes to the assignments.      

We can visualize what these classes look like by sorting fish by their spring-like population ancestry. The 'Spring' class is defined by 1.0--0.6 spring ancestry, the 'Hybrid' class by 0.6--0.4 spring ancestry, and the 'Fall' class by 0.4--0.0 spring ancestry.    

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.width=13, fig.height=3}
tbl2s <- 
  arrange(tbl2, desc(V1)) |>
  mutate(
    ASSIGNMENT=ifelse(grepl("_Spring_", pop), yes="Spring", no=NA), 
    ASSIGNMENT=ifelse(grepl("_Unknown_", pop), yes="Unknown", no=ASSIGNMENT), 
    ASSIGNMENT=ifelse(grepl("_Fall_", pop), yes="Fall", no=ASSIGNMENT), 
    BASELINE=ifelse(grepl("_Baseline", pop), yes=TRUE, no=FALSE),
    Q=cut(V1, breaks=c(0, 0.4, 0.6, 1)))

tbl2s$Q <- 
  factor(
    tbl2s$Q, 
    levels=c("(0.6,1]", "(0.4,0.6]", "(0,0.4]"), 
    labels=c("Spring", "Hybrid", "Fall"), 
    ordered=TRUE)

tbl2s$ASSIGNMENT <- 
  factor(
    tbl2s$ASSIGNMENT, 
    levels=c("Spring", "Unknown", "Fall"), 
    ordered=TRUE)

# pdf("../admixture/gdatw2_k2_sorted.pdf", width=13, height=3)
par(mar=c(7, 4, 4, 2) + 0.1)
barplot(t(as.matrix(tbl2s[1:2])), col=hcl.colors(3)[c(1, 3)], ylab="Ancestry", border=NA, names.arg=tbl2s$pop, las=2, cex.names=0.3, space=0, main=expression(italic(K)==2*`*`), font.main=1)
# abline(h=0.5, v=1026, col="white", lty=3)
abline(h=c(0.4, 0.6), v=c(952.5, 1062.5), , col="white")
mtext(text="'Spring'", adj=0.37)
mtext(text="'Hybrid'", adj=0.76)
mtext(text="'Fall'", adj=0.87)
# dev.off()
```

  

```{r, echo=FALSE, eval=FALSE}

```

##### Ancestry classification of 100% baseline samples

Let's cross-tabulate the GSI assignments with the ancestry classifications. We start by comparing the baseline reporting groupings ('Spring' or 'Fall') with the ancestry classes ('Spring', 'Hybrid', or 'Fall').  The baseline reporting group counts are in rows and the ancestry classes in columns. So for example, 214 fish from the 'Spring' baseline reporting group were also classified as 'Spring' by ancestry, whereas 11 of the fish from the 'Spring' baseline reporting group were classified as 'Hybrid' by their ancestry. Keep in mind, these are 100% baseline fish in this case (the reference samples which we base GSI of mixtures on).  


```{r, echo=FALSE}
table(filter(tbl2s, BASELINE==TRUE)$ASSIGNMENT, filter(tbl2s, BASELINE==TRUE)$Q)[-2, ]
```


It looks like the two baseline reporting groups correspond to 'Spring' and 'Fall' ancestry classes reasonably well. For example, only one 'Fall' reporting group baseline fish was classified as 'Spring' by it's ancestry.  On the other hand, several fish were classified as 'Hybrid' although they are from the 'Spring' or 'Fall' baseline reporting group.


##### Ancestry classification of 100% White River NORs

Let's compare results for the White River NOR fish with the ancestry classes same as above.      

```{r, echo=FALSE}
table(filter(tbl2s, BASELINE==FALSE)$ASSIGNMENT, filter(tbl2s, BASELINE==FALSE)$Q)
```

White River NOR assignment counts (Rubias) are in rows and the ancestry classification counts (ADMIXTURE) are in columns.  We see n=712 'Spring'-assigned fish are also classified as 'Spring' by their ancestry, whereas n=29 of the 'Spring'-assigned fish are classified as 'Hybrid' by their ancestry.  

For the n=36 'Unknown' fish (i.e., fish with posterior probability of GSI assignment to 'Spring' or 'Fall' reporting groups <0.8), we see that almost half (n=17) of these fish are classified as either pure 'Spring' (n=15) or pure 'Fall' (n=2).  

Results for the n=58 'Fall'-assigned fish are interesting. We see that most of the 'Fall'-assigned fish are classified as either 'Hybrid' (n=33) or pure 'Spring' (n=10) by their ancestry.

##### Ancestry Model of White River NORs

Let's see if ADMIXTURE can put the White River NORs into 2 ancestral populations. In other words, lets see if there's any support for splitting these phenotypically spring-run fish (i.e., all returned between Jun-01 and Aug-09) into 'Spring' and 'Fall' populations.     

```{r, echo=FALSE}
ggplot(rdat |> filter(!is.na(day), year %in% 2021:2024), aes(x=day, fill=assignment)) + 
  geom_bar(width=1) + 
  labs(title="White River NOR Genetic Stock Assignments 2021-2024", x=NULL) + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=day_breaks$day, labels=day_breaks$label) +
  scale_fill_manual(name=NULL, values=hcl.colors(3))

NOR <- 
  mutate(gdatw, population=gdatw_pop) |>
  filter(grepl(pattern="White_R", population)) |>
  filter(!grepl(pattern="Baseline", population))

# write_delim(mutate(NOR[-509], ID=paste0("i", ID)), col_names=FALSE, file="../admixture/NOR3.ped", na="0")
# 
# data.frame(Chromosome=1, SNP=paste0("rs", 10001:10251), GD=0, POS=seq(1, 251000000, 1000000)) |> 
#   write_delim(col_names=FALSE, file="../admixture/NOR3.map")
```



```{bash, eval=FALSE}
plink --file NOR3 --make-bed --out NOR3

for K in 1 2 3 4; do admixture -s $RANDOM --cv=10 NOR3.bed $K | tee NOR3_log${K}.out; done

grep -h CV NOR3_log*  > NOR3_log.txt
```

There is little support for these White River NORs to have ancestry from more than one ancestral population when the Green River origin fall run run fish are excluded.  

```{r, echo=FALSE}
NOR_cv <- 
  read_delim("../admixture/NOR3_log.txt", col_names=FALSE) %>% 
  mutate(K=1:nrow(.)) |> 
  select(K, CV_error=X4)

par(mar=c(5, 4, 4, 2) + 0.1)

plot(NOR_cv); lines(NOR_cv)
```

But let's plot ${K} = 2$ barplot just in case there's some interesting pattern to see. 

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.width=13, fig.height=6}

NOR_1 <- read.table("../admixture/NOR3.1.Q")

NOR_2 <- read.table("../admixture/NOR3.2.Q")

NOR_1$id <- 
  NOR$ID

NOR_2$id <- 
  NOR$ID

NOR_1$pop <- 
  NOR$population

NOR_2$pop <- 
  NOR$population

NOR_2 <- 
  bind_rows(NOR_2, tibble(V1=rep(NA, 2), V2=rep(NA, 2)))

rownames(NOR_2)[836:837] <-
  paste0("spacer", 1:2)

NOR_2 <-
  NOR_2[rownames(NOR_2)[c(1:741, 836, 742:777, 837, 778:835)], ]

# pdf("../admixture/NOR3_k2_3.pdf", width=12, height=6)
par(mar=c(7, 4, 4, 2) + 0.1, mfrow=c(2, 1))
barplot(t(as.matrix(data.frame(V1=c(rep(1, 741), NA, rep(1, length(742:777)), NA, rep(1, length(778:835)))))), col=hcl.colors(3)[1], ylab="Ancestry", border=NA, names.arg=NOR_2$pop, las=2, cex.names=0.3, space=0, main=expression(italic(K)==1*`*`), font.main=1)
abline(v=c(742, 779), col="white")
mtext(text="'Spring'", adj=0.47)
mtext(text="?", adj=0.88)
mtext(text="'Fall'", adj=0.94)
barplot(t(as.matrix(NOR_2[1:2])), col=hcl.colors(3)[-2], ylab="Ancestry", border=NA, xaxt="n", las=2, cex.names=0.3, space=0, main=expression(italic(K)==2), font.main=1)
abline(v=c(742, 779), col="white")
mtext(text="'Spring'", adj=0.47)
mtext(text="?", adj=0.88)
mtext(text="'Fall'", adj=0.94)
# dev.off()
```

I don't see anything interesting in the NOR-only ${K} = 2$ barplot.  

But I do think it's interesting how ancestry of these phenotypically-spring run NORs with 'Unknown' and 'Fall' run GSI assignments appears more fall-like when the phenotypically-fall run baseline fish are included. I wonder if that's an artifact of incomplete sampling of ancestral diversity with the closest ancestor unsampled. For instance, a scenario like long branch attraction (LBA) in phylogenetics, where use of an outgroup that's too divergent from your ingroup can cause topology artifacts.
